title: Swinging in the States: Does disinformation on Twitter mirror the US presidential election system?
screen_reason: Twitter study of the week before the 2020 US presidential election (27 October - 3 November 2020) in which every URL shared in the election-debate corpus was tagged by NewsGuard domain reputation. Table 4 reports the share of shared URLs pointing to non-trustworthy news domains separately for swing-state and safe-state tweets (23.47% and 18.33%), each with a stated URL denominator. Because the denominator is links SHARED in tweets and retweets, this is SHARING (content_share), not CONTENT.

estimates.country: United States (tweets mentioning the swing states Arizona, Florida, Michigan, Pennsylvania)
estimates.date: 27 October - 3 November 2020 (the week immediately preceding the US presidential election)
estimates.measure_type: % of URLs shared in swing-state 2020 US election tweets that point to non-trustworthy news domains (NewsGuard tag N)
estimates.value_raw: N = 23.47 (Table 4, row Swing); T (trustworthy) = 29.84 for the same denominator of 352,606 URLs
estimates.denominator: 352,606 URLs contained in 2,911,735 tweets and retweets by 636,125 users that mention exactly one swing state (Arizona, Florida, Michigan or Pennsylvania) together with a candidate name (Trump or Biden), in the network-validated dataset
estimates.definition: URL whose second-level domain carries NewsGuard's 'N' (non-trustworthy news domain) tag; platform links (tag P) and satire (tag S) were excluded from consideration, but domains NewsGuard has not rated (tag UNC) appear to remain in the denominator
estimates.misinfo_def: "For evaluating the credibility level, the Newsguard metrics consider, e.g., whether the news source regularly publishes false news, does not distinguish between facts and opinions, does not correct a wrongly reported news. For transparency, instead, the toolkit takes into account, e.g., whether owners, founders or authors of the news source are publicly known, and whether advertisements are easily recognizable."
estimates.source_quote: Considering links pointing to non-trustworthy news sites (N), the concentration for swing states - 23.47% - is higher than that for safe ones - 18.33%. The concentration of trustworthy links (T) is higher for safe states - 50.87% vs 29.84% for swings.
estimates.page_loc: Section 3.5 'Reputation of news domains in tweets associated to swing and safe states', p. 1401; values also in Table 4 (Swing: No. Users 636125, No. Tweets 2911735, No. URL 352606, T 29.84, N 23.47; Safe: 214329, 404182, 45989, 50.87, 18.33)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Domain-level tagging by NewsGuard (T trustworthy, N non-trustworthy, P platform, S satire, UNC unclassified), applied after expanding all short-form URLs to their second-level domains. NewsGuard's criteria combine credibility (does the source regularly publish false news, separate fact from opinion, correct errors) and transparency (are owners/authors publicly known, are ads recognisable). No item-level verification and no coder reliability applicable. Bot classification (separate analysis) used BotometerLite v4 with the first and last deciles of the bot-score distribution.
estimates.moderator_quote: All the domains in our validated Twitter dataset have been tagged according to their degree of credibility and transparency, as indicated by the browser extension and mobile app NewsGuard. ... Tags T and N in Table 3 are used only for news sites, be them newspapers, magazines, TV or radio social channels, and they stand for Trustworthy and Non-trustworthy, respectively.
estimates.notes: Denominator caveat that drives confidence down to medium: T (29.84) + N (23.47) sums to only 53.31, so roughly 47% of the swing-state URL denominator is made up of links NewsGuard has not rated (UNC). The 23.47% is therefore a share of ALL shared links, not of rated NEWS links; among rated news links only it would be 23.47/53.31 = 44%, but the paper never states that and computing it would breach R8. Two further notes: (a) the paper's own word 'concentration' here means frequency, not the review's CONCENTRATION construct; (b) the denominator is the network-validated dataset (tweets by users affiliated with the political communities that emerge from a Bipartite Configuration Model filter, which discards about 17% of tweets, roughly 64k), not the raw 5.3M-tweet collection, so this is the share within politically engaged accounts.

estimates.notes: Same UNC-in-denominator caveat as the swing row: T (50.87) + N (18.33) = 69.2, leaving about 31% unrated. Kept as a separate row rather than folded into the swing row because swing-vs-safe IS this paper's headline comparison and no pooled figure is reported; pooling them myself (which would give 22.9%) would be a cross-category computation barred by R8.

missed_or_uncertain: Considered and NOT extracted, with the bot result being the one an adjudicator should look at hardest. (a) BOTS AS A CONCENTRATION ROW. The paper reports that 'Out of the total number of classified accounts, bots account for 47.19%' and that bots posted or retweeted 73.69% of non-trustworthy links overall (74.15% in swing states, 68.75% in safe states; Table 6), plus 'Out of the total traffic from classified accounts, bots produce 64.19% of the traffic.' Mechanically this satisfies R1 (a group percentage AND their share of sharing: conc_group_pct 47.19, conc_share_pct 73.69, conc_unit user, conc_dimension sharing), but I did NOT create a CONCENTRATION row because the review defines CONCENTRATION as a TOP group of users ranked by activity, and 'bots' is an account-type split, not a top-activity group. The 47.19% is also computed over a heavily restricted base: only accounts in the first and last deciles of the BotometerLite score (57,797 human + 51,648 bot = 109,445 accounts, sharing 78,439 URLs) - everyone in deciles 2-9 is dropped, so bots are ~10% of the validated accounts but 47% of the CLASSIFIED ones. A concentration row built from these two numbers would mix denominators. If the review wants it, all the pieces are here. (b) '88% of the entire traffic can be associated with swing states' - a distribution of election traffic across state types, not a misinformation share. (c) Table 6's link-type percentages (all links 89.92% swing / 10.08% safe; non-trustworthy links 91.53% swing / 8.47% safe) describe where non-trustworthy links were shared, i.e. within-misinformation composition, not prevalence. (d) Bot-score distribution details (first decile 0-0.04, last decile 0.45-1) and Table 5 counts are method descriptors. (e) A non-trustworthy share for the decile-restricted subset could be computed as 20,627/78,439 = 26.3% (Table 6), but it is not stated verbatim and its denominator is the artificial decile subset, so it is not extracted. (f) Prevalence figures quoted from other papers (e.g. Allcott/Gentzkow-style fake-news sharing counts, Grinberg, Eady) are barred by R8.

rob.design: Observational Twitter study. Collection: Streaming Twitter API, about 5.3M tweets over 27 October - 3 November 2020, driven by 16 keyword pairs combining each of eight state names with each candidate (Trump, Biden). States chosen from political analysts' reports: four swing (Arizona 11, Florida 29, Michigan 16, Pennsylvania 20 electors) and four safe, balanced by party and electors (Washington and New Jersey = 26 Democratic electors; Indiana and Louisiana = 19 Republican). Processing: English-only; tweets naming more than one of the eight states discarded, so each tweet maps to exactly one state type; short URLs expanded to second-level domains; resulting dataset about 3.3M tweets and about 398k URLs (Table 2). Filtering: retweet interactions between verified and unverified users modelled as a bipartite network, validated against a Bipartite Configuration Model null model, projected onto the verified layer, Louvain community detection, communities manually labelled from their verified members, then labels propagated to unverified users (Raghavan label propagation); tweets by users not affiliated with a political community discarded as noise - about 17% of tweets (roughly 64k) dropped. Resulting retweet network: 547k nodes, 1.8M edges; the largest community is mainly Republican supporters, the second mixed. Link reputation: NewsGuard domain tags (T/N/P/S/UNC), with P and S excluded from consideration. Bot detection: BotometerLite (Botometer v4 premium, profile-features-only), accounts ranked by bot score with only the first decile (0-0.04, 'genuine') and last decile (0.45-1, 'bot') retained for the bot analysis. No human annotation of individual tweets for veracity; the authors note as a limitation that, being keyword-driven, 'we do not know a priori the exact content of the collected tweets', and that only 8 states and one election year are covered.
